content: 1. The evidence was downgraded by two levels due to imprecision. This was because there were few events, and the 95% confidence interval included both a potentially harmful effect and a potentially beneficial effect of the intervention. 2. The evidence was downgraded by one level due to risk of bias. This was attributed to unclear randomization sequence generation and allocation concealment, lack of blinding for participants and providers, incomplete outcome data, and selective outcome reporting. 3. The evidence was downgraded by one level for imprecision. The 95% confidence interval encompassed both a potential small harmful effect and a potential small beneficial effect of the intervention. 4. The evidence was downgraded by two levels for imprecision. This was due to a small sample size, which resulted in wide confidence intervals that included harm, no effect, and benefit of the intervention. 5. The results were non-comparable, leading to a downgrade to very low certainty. 6. Digital, targeted client communication for adult users of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, compared to standard care in primary healthcare settings, was assessed. The patient population included adult users or potential users of SRH services in community settings across high-income countries (Australia, UK, USA) and middle-income countries (Bangladesh, Cameroon, Kenya, India, Cambodia, South Africa, Brazil, Colombia, China, Uganda). 7. The intervention involved targeted client communication, such as reminders and/or information/education delivered via SMS, MMS, IVR, instant messaging, app-based messaging, or voice calls. The comparison was standard care or no intervention. 8. The certainty of evidence for clinic attendance for STI/HIV testing among adults was assessed as very low. This was based on studies conducted in community settings in Australia, Kenya, and the UK. 9. The certainty of evidence for clinic attendance for HIV treatment among adults was also assessed as very low. This was based on studies conducted in community settings in the USA and Cameroon. 10. The intervention probably slightly increases the number of women attending post-abortion care. However, the range of the actual effect suggests that the intervention may have little or no effect or may slightly increase attendance. This was based on a study conducted in a community setting in South Africa. 11. The intervention may make little or no difference in the number of men attending clinics for voluntary medical male circumcision. This was based on a study conducted in community settings. 12. The intervention may increase contraception use at four months among women. This was based on a study conducted in a community setting in Cambodia. 13. The intervention may increase contraception use at 12 months among women. This was also based on a study conducted in a community setting in Cambodia. 14. The certainty of evidence for the effect of the intervention on condom use among adults was assessed as very low. This was based on a study conducted in a community setting in the USA. 15. The intervention may increase adherence to antiretroviral medication among adults living with HIV and AIDS. This was based on studies conducted in community settings in Brazil, India, Kenya, and Cameroon. 16. The intervention may make little or no difference to health status among individuals living with HIV and AIDS, as assessed by CD4 count. This was based on studies conducted in community settings in China and Cameroon. 17. The World Health Organization (WHO) no longer recommends the use of CD4 count to monitor response to antiretroviral therapy (ART) or to diagnose treatment failure. Instead, viral load measurements are recommended. 18. The certainty of evidence for the effect of the intervention on HIV viral load among individuals living with HIV and AIDS was assessed as very low. This was based on studies conducted in community settings in Kenya and India. 19. The intervention may make little or no difference to well-being among individuals living with HIV and AIDS, as measured by SF-12 or WHO Quality of Life physical well-being subscales. This was based on studies conducted in community settings in China and Cameroon. 20. The certainty of evidence for the effect of the intervention on the number of repeat abortions following an earlier abortion was assessed as very low. This was based on a study conducted in a community setting in Cambodia. 21. Client satisfaction and acceptance of the intervention were generally reported as moderate to high across all studies. However, only the intervention group was assessed for this outcome, making the results non-comparable. 22. No studies were identified that reported on providers' acceptance or satisfaction with the intervention. Therefore, the effect of the intervention on this outcome remains uncertain. 23. The intervention may increase the number of women who experience physical violence. This was based on a study conducted in a community setting in Bangladesh. 24. Three studies reported on unintended consequences of the intervention. One study explicitly reported no adverse events, while another reported that one female participant withdrew because she felt the intervention compromised her undisclosed status. A third study reported no involvement in road traffic accidents or domestic abuse as a result of the intervention. 25. The WHO defines viral failure as a persistently detectable viral load exceeding 1,000 copies/mL (based on two consecutive measurements within a three-month interval with adherence support) after at least six months of ART. Treatment success is defined as two consecutive viral load measurements below 1,000 copies/mL.
